passages.text: A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must maintain a position while we look at a target. An animal moving through an environment must represent where it is. How do groups of nerve cells perform these tasks when their electrical signals are brief and variable?

These questions belong to computational and systems neuroscience: explaining how groups of neurons, the brain's signaling cells, represent information and support behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions; recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement. The three papers use these methods to study different parts of the problem: maintaining a value, locating the source of an irregular movement, and explaining the spatial patterns through which cells represent position.

Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists. The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals.

Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander. Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 2 and 3 derive the result and its limits.[^orientation-memory]

Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It changes the image reaching the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.

They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapter 4 separates the measured relationships, the statistical inference and the proposed mechanism.[^orientation-eye]

A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations. Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.

Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapter 5 develops the model and distinguishes exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical tests.[^orientation-place]

The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in Chapter 6.

The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra. Neuroscience terms and the required stochastic-process, information, filtering, and random-field ideas are taught where needed. The first chapter establishes spikes, population activity, fixed points, covariance, and diffusion. Chapters 2 and 3 derive the persistent-activity model and its information bound. Chapter 4 applies the dynamical ideas to eye drift. Chapter 5 develops spatial Gaussian processes and place-field geometry. Chapter 6 brings the results together and compares related work.

For the memory and eye papers, follow chapters 1 through 4 in order. For place fields, the relevant starting path is chapter 1 followed by chapter 5; its Gaussian-process calculation does not require every readout result in chapter 3. The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.
After the foundations, the [guide map](../chapters/ch-foundations.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) shows the three paper questions together.

On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions; open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

The central theory is derived step by step. Examples chosen for the guide distinguish independent from shared fluctuations, complete from limited access to neural signals, and exact formulas from approximations for rare fields. Their numbers are checked separately from the published experimental measurements. A teaching reconstruction is labeled when its simplified model differs from the paper's full model.

The guide explains how to interpret the experiments and their figures. It does not rerun the original animal recordings, data processing, or full neural-network simulations. A successful numerical check of a probability identity is different from an independent reproduction of a paper's empirical result. Related work is selected to clarify the assumptions and alternatives rather than to claim an exhaustive literature search.

Throughout the guide, $D$ denotes the [**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads. In the basic one-dimensional model, $D$ is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its [**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time $t$, is $2Dt$. Chapter 1 explains this model and its assumptions. The symbol $d$ denotes spatial dimension. The memory chapters use $\theta$ for a represented coordinate. The place-field chapter uses $q$ for normalized threshold, which the paper calls $\theta$, and $C$ for its spatial covariance. Each chapter states further symbols and units before its equations depend on them.

The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system. The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns.

The first distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory]

A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s. A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time. A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds.

Neurons affect one another through connections called [**synapse**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s. In the models used here, an excitatory input increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire and an inhibitory input reduces it. The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has [**recurrent connectivity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears.

A [**tuning curve**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} gives a neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable. For eye angle $\theta$, a simple local model is $r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta$. Neuron $i$ has baseline rate $b_i$ in spikes per second and slope $k_i$ in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.[^f-eye]
Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector

is a [**population code**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: the pattern across $N$ neurons carries information about $\theta$. The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. Reading a value from observed spikes is [**decoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Establishing a population pattern from an input is encoding. The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity.

Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. One neuron can have several fields. A [**rate map**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there. Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model's expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.[^f-place]

The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells. CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation. CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation. A [**grid cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena. These repeated grid fields and a place cell's irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1's output maps need not identify where the animal's position estimate is maintained.[^f-anatomy]

Even when the represented value stays fixed, the spikes need not repeat from trial to trial. The 2012 model starts with a tractable description of this variability: a [**Poisson process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. At constant rate $r$, the number $K$ of spikes in an interval of length $\Delta t$ obeys
Here $\lambda$ is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution,
The variance follows directly from the first two factorial moments. Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$,

The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is $\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda$. This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.[^f-poisson]
[**Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population**]{#sec-foundations-count-example}

Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is $20\times0.05=1$. The probability of seeing no spike is $e^{-1}=0.368$. A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive.

Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{20}=4.47$. The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If cells share an additional fluctuating drive, that common variation will not disappear in the same way.
The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale.

For changing rates, the expected count is the integral $\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt$. In a recurrent network, $r(t)$ itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the evolving state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains.

Other measurements describe other aspects of variability. The [**coefficient of variation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, or CV, of interspike intervals is their standard deviation divided by their mean. A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022. The count variance divided by mean count is the [**Fano factor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}; its value also depends on the counting interval. CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions.

To identify where variability enters a pathway, the eye paper compares measurements that share some fluctuations and have other fluctuations of their own. The required probability identities are short, but their interpretation matters.
For random variables $X$ and $Y$, [**covariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures how their centered values vary together:
It has units equal to the product of the units of $X$ and $Y$. Variance is the special case $\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)$. Expanding a centered sum or difference gives

Independence makes the covariance zero when the relevant moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence in general. The [**correlation coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} rescales covariance:

It has no units and lies between $-1$ and $1$ for variables with nonzero variance. The magnitude of a correlation is not automatically the fraction of an output variance caused by a particular source. Establishing that interpretation requires a model of the signal, noise, and measurement gains. Chapter 4 supplies that model for eye displacement.

Thus a growing mean squared displacement can contain random spread, a systematic change in the mean, or both. This identity will distinguish random memory diffusion from a biased or leaky integrator.

A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero. It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays.

Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model. The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit. A line attractor has one represented coordinate; a ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory]

Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. In the continuous diffusion approximation this becomes

The [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$ starts at zero, has independent Gaussian increments, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$. It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. The parameter $D$ is its [**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It measures the rate of variance growth; a single trajectory need not move monotonically away from its starting value.

The [**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate. In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.

A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit.

These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields. The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.[^f-place]
The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.

A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied. The important question is whether the activity pattern stays in the right place, not just whether activity continues. Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set. This chapter derives how random spikes move the network along that set. The next chapter asks how well another network can read the moving memory.[^p1-model]

Paper and Supporting Information (SI) links open the cited PDF page, near the passage where the viewer supports it. Use the equation, figure, or paragraph label to find the passage; the PDFs have no numbered text lines.

The memory coordinate is $\theta$. Its initial value is $\Theta$. A bar denotes a noise free steady state, so $\bar r_i(\theta)$ is neuron $i$'s steady firing rate at memory value $\theta$. The common synaptic time constant is $\tau$. A one dimensional diffusion coefficient $D$ has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention $\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt$ when $D$ is constant and boundaries do not matter.

How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]

This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.

The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in Chapters 1 and 2 stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.[^p2-recordings]

There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: a changing shared command sent to many OMNs, private spike variability in individual OMNs, and variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging. This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement.

The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. The animals first fixated a stationary target and then tracked a moving target. A wire search coil on one eye measured eye position while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.[^p2-recordings][^p2-single]

The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]

The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect [**gain**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.

Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. The cell fires where this function exceeds a threshold. The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.[^p3-question]

This chapter develops the calculations behind that claim. Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.

To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram.

A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector. For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions,

The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. A jointly Gaussian vector is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian. For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model]

Three assumptions have different jobs. [**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation. It does not say that a particular map is flat. [**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$. It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. Finally, smoothness controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives. Crossing calculations below require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below.

A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. The three papers become more useful together when these different claims are kept attached to their actual mathematical and experimental tests.

For a circuit representing position, three questions arise. What activity pattern corresponds to each position? How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The place-field model addresses the first question. The persistent-activity model addresses the second. The eye-drift model combines a candidate answer to the second with a detailed answer to the third.[^s-three]

In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, $x$ locates an animal in an environment, and $h_i(x)$ is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered $x$ through time.

A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. The place-field paper gains support by fitting arrangement parameters and then comparing additional features, including slices and shape statistics. The separate firing-rate multiplier used in some comparisons should remain visible when counting how many quantities were predicted without further fitting. A successful high-threshold formula is also a statement about its limiting assumptions; finite-threshold simulations and the original recordings provide different kinds of checks.

The eye paper uses a different strategy. It calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. Shared covariance then carries information that independent private fluctuations cannot supply under the decomposition's assumptions. The additional MSD comparison tests the time structure: increasing stationary motor-noise amplitude cannot by itself reproduce the accumulating upstream signal. Calibration validity, source correlations, two animals, and horizontal movement remain part of the result's scope.

The 2012 inequality is a mathematical constraint rather than an experimental fit. Its derivation specifies what noise and dynamics it covers. An experimental comparison would need estimates of diffusion, the relevant time constants, and the appropriate instantaneous information rate, all under compatible conditions. Agreement with $1/N$ scaling alone would not test the entire inequality, since several mechanisms can share that scaling.

The foundational eye-position account is Seung's line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete's earlier grid-cell study puts a related integrator problem in navigation: recurrent population activity is driven by velocity and accumulates path-integration errors. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.[^s-attractors]

Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior; transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.[^s-extensions]

For place fields, Eliav and colleagues' long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues' large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.[^s-place-data]

There are also direct reasons to avoid reading Gaussian spatial statistics as a unique wiring diagram. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in dendrites, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model's success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.[^s-wiring]

Finally, the source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.[^s-acuity]

The combined calculation suggests a concrete research direction. For the same population, first estimate the tuning maps with their uncertainty. Then measure fluctuations during periods where external anchoring is weak and test whether their covariance is aligned with changes along those maps. Fit diffusion only over a range where the local approximation and measurement corrections are justified. A downstream behavioral comparison must additionally include the physical or neural filters between representation and measurement.

This would ask whether one system satisfies both spatial-statistics and dynamical-stability constraints. A static Gaussian-process fit alone cannot supply the diffusion coefficient. A diffusion fit alone cannot establish the distribution of fields. A joint success would be more restrictive, while a mismatch would point to a particular assumption to change: spatial input statistics, recurrent maintenance, the observation filter, or their coupling. This is proposed follow-up work, not a replication claimed by this guide.
